21.0.0.en: 1 The king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will. 2 Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts. 3 To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice. 4 A haughty look and a swelling heart, the light of the wicked, is sin.

21.0.1.en: The king’s heart is in the hand of the LORD, as the rivers of water: he turneth it whithersoever he will [1].

21.0.2.en: On the last night of the kingdom of Babylon, the prophet Daniel wanted to reveal to King Belshazzar that God is behind the rise of every kingdom, and that He has a special plan for the life of every king. This is the God whose house’s vessels Belshazzar had defiled (Dan 5:1-4), so he said to him: “O thou king, the most high God gave Nebuchadnezzar thy father a kingdom, and majesty, and glory, and honour...” (Dan 5:18, etc.).

21.0.3.en: All kings, the pious and the wicked, believers and unbelievers, will not move without God’s permission or will. Many of them think that they are able to work on a worldwide level, such as Pharaoh of Egypt, the kings of Assyria and Babylon, the Caesars of Rome, Alexander the Great and Napoleon Bonaparte. They did not know that they could not act without God’s permission. They declared, openly or secretly, their independence from God. This is what many leaders, and indeed many of the people, feel: that they do as they please. We need to celebrate daily our declaration of dependence on Almighty God, and not our independence from Him.

21.0.4.en: Esther realized this and cried out with her people, and the Lord moved the king’s heart, as is told throughout the whole book, especially when the king’s sleep fled from him and he read in the book of the records of the chronicles what Mordecai had done, and events moved on behalf of the people of God (Dan 6).

21.0.5.en: The hand of God moved Cyrus the Persian, for it is said: “Thus saith the LORD to his anointed, to Cyrus, whose right hand I have holden, to subdue nations before him...”

21.0.6.en: If this is God’s work even with wicked kings, how much more is His role in the lives of His believers, as He says to the prophet Jeremiah: “Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee; and before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations” (Jer 1:5).

21.0.7.en: As the One who weighs the hearts, He is the only physician specialized in mending the heart and renewing it. Therefore we cry out to Him at the beginning of the prayer in every hour: “Create in me a clean heart, O God” (Ps 51).

21.0.8.en: Who is the king whose heart is in the hand of the Lord? 1. The righteous leader: every righteous leader feels that his leading role does not rest on attaining a certain position, whether at the level of society or the Church, or work or the family, etc., but is realized when he acquires within himself a kingly heart, by his union with the Lord, the King of kings. The leader walks in humility and surrender in the hands of God, who directs his heart, his mind, his feelings and his sensations. His leading role is in truth walking according to the will of God, his Leader. 2. The wicked leader: some see that God permits him in order to discipline the wicked who are subject to him and to prove the children of God, so God uses him for edification. In this way his heart is in the hand of the Lord. This is as was said of Nebuchadnezzar and other kings who humbled the people of God in order to discipline them, so that Nebuchadnezzar, the pagan and wicked, was called the servant of the Lord. 3. Every holy soul is counted in the eyes of God a queen or a king, as the beloved St. John says: “And hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father” (Rev 1:6). The wise man says: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (Wis 3:1).

21.0.9.en: * Surrender your soul into the hands of the Lord. Not only when you depart from the body, but also when you are in the body, it is in the hands of the Lord, even if you do not see it, nor see its source, nor the place of its arrival. It is in you and with the Lord. Therefore “the king’s heart is in the hand of the Lord,” who leads it and rules over it. The heart is also full of the Spirit, for the spirit is the governing part in the soul, and it is the power of the soul. I say that strength does not lie in the arms, but in counsel, in self-control, in godliness and in justice. If the heart of man is in the hand of the Lord, how much more is his soul.

21.0.10.en: St. Ambrose * If “the king’s heart is in the hand of God,” then he is not saved by the strength of arms but by divine leading. Now not just any man at random is in the hand of God, but one who is worthy of the name of king.

21.0.11.en: St. Basil the Great * Surely the prophet is not referring to the kings of this world, since it is written: “The king’s heart is in the hand of God.”

21.0.12.en: Do you suppose even for a moment that the heart of Julian the Apostate is in the hand of God? Far from it!

21.0.13.en: Or the heart of Nero, or Maximian, or Decius, the persecutors? Far from it!

21.0.14.en: He is speaking of those who rule over sin; now these have their hearts in the hand of God, they triumph over vices and the lusts of their souls and overcome sin.

21.0.15.en: * Are the hearts of Julian the persecutor, or Nero, or Decius in the hand of God? No!

21.0.16.en: The hearts that are in the hand of God are the hearts of those who master their bodies, subdue them and bring them into bondage, lest when they have preached to others they themselves should be cast away (1 Cor 9:27).

21.0.17.en: These are the kings of whom Wisdom speaks in the book of Proverbs: [“He gives kingship to kings”] (cf. Prov 8:15).

21.0.18.en: St. Jerome * God alone knows the secrets of man. Hear what the prophet says: “Thou only knowest the hearts” (2 Chr 6:30), and also: “God searcheth the hearts and reigneth” (Mk 7:9), and Jeremiah says: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and it is man, who can know it?” (Prov 21:9). “Man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1 Sam 16:7).

21.0.19.en: * The knowledge of the secrets of men belongs to God alone... “The heart is deep beyond all things, and it is man, who can know it?” (Prov 21:9) LXX.

21.1.0.en: St. John Chrysostom Every way of a man is right in his own eyes: but the LORD pondereth the hearts [2].

21.1.1.en: The first obstacle to harmony with the good will of God is man’s justifying himself, so that he thinks that everything he thinks and everything he does is right. Therefore the Apostle Paul says: “For I know nothing by myself; yet am I not hereby justified: but he that judgeth me is the Lord” (1 Cor 4:4).

21.1.2.en: A man justifies his position before himself as well as before men, but he cannot justify himself before God, who weighs and searches the hearts. The prophet Jeremiah says: “The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it?” (Jer 17:9).

21.1.3.en: * Are not those who condemn their sins better true Christians than those who think of defending them? The righteous man is the first accuser of himself (Prov 18:17). He who accuses himself when he sins is righteous, and not he who praises himself.

21.1.4.en: St. Ambrose As the One who weighs the hearts, God cares for the uprightness of our hearts, their widening with true love and their being marked by mercy, so He says: “I will have mercy, and not sacrifice” (Hos 6:6; Mt 9:13; Mt 12:7).

21.1.5.en: * The doors are opened to every person who returns to God in truth and with all his heart, and the all-joyful Father receives His truly repentant son. True repentance is no longer to be tied to the sins he has renounced... but to uproot them completely from his soul. By their being uprooted God makes His dwelling in you. For it was said that there is great, overflowing joy, and a feast in the heavenly places with the Father and the angels, when a sinner returns and repents. This is the reason for which He cries out, “I will have mercy, and not sacrifice.”

21.2.0.en: St. Clement of Alexandria To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice [3].

21.2.1.en: If God is the hidden Leader, then it is fitting for the believer to know His will through His word, in order to walk according to His divine will.

21.2.2.en: * God Himself says that He prefers obedience to His commandments over the offering of sacrifices to God. God declares this, and Moses proclaims it to the people of Israel, and Paul preaches this to the Gentiles. Do what you see to be best at present.

21.3.0.en: St. Ambrose A haughty look and a swelling heart, the light of the wicked, is sin [4].

21.3.1.en: If the word of God supports the believer, as a king, so that God reigns over his heart and leads him according to His divine will, then the most dangerous enemy that corrupts the heart is the high eyes and the proud heart, even if a man presents works that seem glorious, or a light, unless he returns to God in the spirit of humility in sincere repentance. If the governor of a province rebelled against the emperor, or against the head of state, then whatever seemingly glorious works he did, he would be branded with rebellion, unless he returned and handed over his weapons to the emperor or the president. This is what the Apostle Paul accused Israel of: “For I bear them record that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge. For they being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God” (Rom 10:2-3).

21.3.2.en: He whose eyes are lifted up over his brethren, so that he looks at them with contempt, even if he does not utter a single word against them, God looks at the works of his self-righteousness as a menstruous rag. As the prophet Isaiah says: “But we are all as an unclean thing, and all our righteousnesses are as filthy rags” (Isa 64:6).

21.3.3.en: * If someone has love toward God, but does not know that love requires one to be patient, kind, not envious, doing no wrong, not puffed up, not covetous, not seeking its own, and so on, then since he does not have these things in his love, but loves God with bare emotions, it is rightly said of him that he has the love of God but not according to knowledge.

21.3.4.en: Origen * Many are led by their own spirit, trusting in their own virtues, content only with hearing the Law without seeking the help of grace; these are not the children of God. Of such the Apostle says: “For they being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God” (Rom 10:3). He said this about the Jews who, in their self-reliance, despised grace and did not believe in Christ.

21.3.5.en: He says that they wanted to establish their own righteousness, this righteousness which is of the Law. Not that they carry out the Law, but they establish their righteousness in the Law when they reckon in themselves that they are able to carry out the Law by their own strength, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, not the righteousness that belongs to the Apostle Paul, but the righteousness that God grants to man.

21.4.s.en: 2. Diligence in the spirit of righteousness

21.4.0.en: 5 The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want. 6 The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a vapor driven away for those who seek death. 7 The robbery of the wicked shall destroy them; because they refuse to do judgment. 8 The way of a perverse man is crooked: but as for the pure, his work is right.

21.4.1.en: The thoughts of the diligent tend only to plenteousness; but of every one that is hasty only to want [5].

21.4.2.en: It is fitting for the believer, as a spiritual leader, to be a living example in his practical conduct, always working with diligence and faithfulness and without haste. Diligence is a virtue, while haste and lack of deliberation is a mistake. It is fitting for the believer in his diligence to know what to do, and when to do it, and to what extent, and even when to stop. It is not fitting for him to waste his time, his energies and his abilities without wisdom. “He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich” (Prov 10:4). “The hand of the diligent shall bear rule: but the slothful shall be under tribute” (Prov 12:24). “The slothful man roasteth not that which he took in hunting: but the substance of a diligent man is precious” (Prov 12:27). “The soul of the sluggard desireth, and hath nothing: but the soul of the diligent shall be made fat” (Prov 13:4).

21.4.3.en: This will not be achieved by haste in work. As the wise man says: “He that hasteth with his feet sinneth” (Prov 19:2). “Seest thou a man that is hasty in his words? there is more hope of a fool than of him” (Prov 29:20).

21.4.4.en: * Everyone must use perfectly everything he has for the common good. If you have wisdom or strength or wealth or anything else, let it not be for the destruction of your fellow servants nor for your own destruction.

21.4.5.en: * Where does the great disparity in the conditions of life come from? From the greed and arrogance of the rich.

21.5.0.en: St. John Chrysostom The getting of treasures by a lying tongue is a vapor driven away for those who seek death [6].

21.5.1.en: Wealth in itself is not evil, but gathering it by lying and deceit in a spirit of greed destroys a man spiritually, socially and sometimes physically. Both Vernon McGee and Henry Ironside, in their commentaries on this phrase, tell the story of the Bedouin who was dying of hunger and found a bag on the path of a caravan, and thought that he would find food in it or cans of fruit juice. He opened it quickly to know what was in it, and was seized by a state of extreme despair as he said: “Alas, they are pearls!” Truly it is a precious treasure, but it cannot satisfy one who is starving!

21.5.2.en: * Observe how there is no dispute over things held in common, but all use them in peace. But as soon as someone tries to acquire something and make it his own possession, dispute appears, as though nature itself protested against this conduct. While God gathers us by every means, we strive to be divided and separated from one another, by appropriating things and using the two cold words “mine and thine.” Then conflicts and hatred appear, and where this does not happen no dispute or conflict appears.

21.5.3.en: * Let us learn from the lessons of true wisdom and say: we do not forbid the seeking of wealth, but we forbid riches acquired in an unlawful way. For it is lawful to be rich, but without greed or plunder or violence, and without a bad reputation among all people.

21.6.0.en: St. John Chrysostom The robbery of the wicked shall destroy them; because they refuse to do judgment [7].

21.6.1.en: A man may acquire much by injustice and robbery, but he loses his life and his happiness, and even perishes, since he refuses to do judgment. God does not accept robbery, even if a man gives what he has robbed to the poor or to the Church.

21.6.2.en: * May we add to our almsgiving, by our prayers, the wings of godliness, and pray that it may fly with greater speed to God. Moreover, the Christian soul realizes the importance of avoiding the theft of the goods of others, by realizing that not sharing what is beyond one’s need with those in need is a kind of theft.

21.6.3.en: St. Augustine * A man’s not giving part of his possessions to others is indeed counted a kind of robbery... The Lord says: “You have taken what belongs to the poor.” He says this to make clear to the rich that what they possess belongs to the poor, even if it is an inheritance from their fathers, or they obtained some money from any source. He says in another place: “Defraud not the poor of his living” (Sir 4:1).

21.6.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * You must avoid the sin of covetousness, not only by refusing to seize what belongs to others, but also by not clinging to your own possessions, which will no longer be yours afterward. The Lord says: “And if ye have not been faithful in that which is another man’s, who shall give you that which is your own?” (Lk 16:12). Gold and silver are not ours; what is ours is the spiritual inheritance.

21.7.0.en: St. Jerome The way of a perverse man is crooked: but as for the pure, his work is right [8].

21.7.1.en: A man’s relationship with God is reflected in his life: if he is rebellious and stubborn, his ways become crooked like the serpent, offering excuses and justifications for his behavior. But he who has fellowship with God walks with the Spirit of God in uprightness, and shrinks from all cunning and crookedness.

21.7.2.en: The Holy Bible presents us with examples of the two kinds. Among those who rebelled was King Ahab, and the people followed him in this course. Therefore (Elijah) “came unto all the people, and said, How long halt ye between two opinions? if the LORD be God, follow him: but if Baal, then follow him” (1 Kgs 18:21). And among those who walked in uprightness was the prophet Daniel, against whom the presidents and princes tried to find an occasion in order to be rid of him, but “they could find none occasion nor fault; forasmuch as he was faithful, neither was there any error or fault found in him” (Dan 6:4).

21.7.3.en: * In truth nothing makes men so foolish as the practice of evil habits: when a man is deceitful, when he is unjust, when he is rude (and these are certainly different forms of doing evil), when he deals painful blows without cause... when he conceals himself in a trick, how does he not show signs of complete folly?

21.7.4.en: St. John Chrysostom * He who builds his house by injustice builds for himself a testimony of destruction.

21.8.0.en: It is better to dwell in a corner of the housetop, than with a brawling woman and a shared house [9].

21.8.1.en: Since the heart of Michal, daughter of Saul, was occupied with vainglory, she could not bear to see her husband David dancing with joy at the bringing of the ark of the covenant to Jerusalem, so she said to him with contempt: “How glorious was the king of Israel to day, who uncovered himself to day in the eyes of the handmaids of his servants, as one of the vain fellows shamelessly uncovereth himself!” (2 Sam 6:20).

21.8.2.en: Another example of a wife who carried a spirit of contention is the wife of Job, who instead of strengthening her husband in the time of affliction said to him: “Dost thou still retain thine integrity? Bless (curse) God, and die” (Job 2:9).

21.8.3.en: Because of the importance of choosing a life partner who is holy in the Lord, this phrase is repeated in (Proverbs 25:24; 21:9).

21.8.4.en: The wise man did not ask the husband to drive out the contentious wife; rather he counts the house as the wife’s, nor did he ask him to divorce her, nor to push her to dwell on the roof of the house, but he himself dwells on the roof, far from foolish quarrels, perhaps she may turn back from the spirit of strife, and the two may live in a spirit of love in peace.

21.8.5.en: * The hearts of those who love have wings... Love can turn into hatred if weighty causes of mutual disrespect creep into it.

21.8.6.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * When the wise man enumerates the things that are counted blessings, he mentions among them “a wife that agreeth with her husband” (Sir 25:1); and in another place he mentions among the blessings that a woman dwell in harmony with her husband (Sir 40:23).

21.8.7.en: In truth, from the beginning God showed a special concern for this unity, and counted the two as one. He said: “Male and female created he them” (Gen 1:27), and it was said: “There is neither male nor female” (Gal 3:28). There is no relationship between one person and another as strong as the relationship that exists between a man and his wife, if they are bound together as they ought to be!

21.8.8.en: Therefore when the wise man wished to express the overflowing love in his grief for a person dear to him... he did not refer to a father or a mother or a son or a brother or a friend, but to whom did he refer? He says: “Thy love to me was wonderful, passing the love of women” (2 Sam 1:26). Truly this love is more violent than any violence, for the other kinds (of love) are strong, but this affection is not only strong, it also does not wither.

21.8.9.en: There is a certain love settled in the depth of our nature, which binds our bodies to one another in a way that cannot be comprehended.

21.8.10.en: From the very beginning the woman came out of the man, and afterward every man and woman comes out of the man and the woman together (1 Cor 11:8).

21.8.11.en: Do you perceive the strength of the bond and the power of the sign?! How God did not allow a foreign nature to intervene from outside. Observe how the provisions were filled with divine care?! For He allowed the man to marry his sister, no, not his sister, but his daughter, not his daughter but what is more than his daughter, she is his body! (Here he refers to the marriage of Adam to Eve.)

21.8.12.en: Thus God created all from one beginning, so that they are joined to one another like stones in a building in one unity.

21.8.13.en: He did not create her from outside, lest the man feel that she is a stranger to him, nor did He stop marriage with her alone, lest she be confined to herself and think that she is the center of all (here he means that she cannot bear children without the man, otherwise she would be proud against him and love would not have arisen between them; rather her feeling of need for him in order to bear fruit makes the children a sign of the union and love between them). There is nothing that joins our lives to one another like the love of a man and his wife.

21.8.14.en: St. John Chrysostom * You prefer dry bread eaten in the desert, and salt and water to drink, to the luxury and pleasures of life in the cities, joined with their cares and anxieties: “Better is a dry morsel, and quietness therewith, than an house full of sacrifices with strife” (Prov 17:1). And the writer of the book of Proverbs, in saying this long ago, was prophesying about you, O monks beloved of God, that you are free from everything. You have no woman to tempt you with her ornaments, nor sons and daughters to weigh you down with their many demands, nor a slave to steal your money and run away with it, nor concerns for riches to deprive you of your sleep, as Ecclesiastes says: “The abundance of the rich will not suffer him to sleep” (Eccl 5:11).

21.8.15.en: St. Anba Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis

21.9.0.en: 10 The soul of the wicked desireth evil: his neighbour findeth no favour in his eyes. 11 When the scorner is punished, the simple is made wise: and when the wise is instructed, he receiveth knowledge. 12 The righteous man considers the house of the wicked, and overthrows the wicked for their wickedness.

21.9.1.en: The soul of the wicked desireth evil.

21.9.2.en: His neighbour findeth no favour in his eyes [10].

21.9.3.en: Man reflects what is in his heart onto what is around him and onto those around him, for “unto the pure all things are pure: but unto them that are defiled and unbelieving is nothing pure” (Titus 1:15). The wicked man sees everything as evil; he does not see a virtuous or godly person, and no one finds favor in his eyes. He does not cease to condemn everyone.

21.9.4.en: * Abba Isaiah said: “If the thought of judging your neighbor because of some fault comes to your mind, first think within yourself that you are a much greater sinner than he, and the good that you believe you are doing, do not suppose that it has pleased God, and in this way you will not be in danger of condemning your neighbor.”

21.9.5.en: * And he also said: “Do not judge your neighbor and despise yourself, and in this way you will feel the peace of conscience.”

21.10.0.en: Garden of the Monks When the scorner is punished, the simple is made wise: and when the wise is instructed, he receiveth knowledge [11].

21.10.1.en: While severity and firmness are needed with reckless criminals so that they may be an example to others, the wise, even if they err, need counsel and guidance, for by the spirit of persuasion and dialogue they can be disciplined. The Apostle Paul used great firmness with the reckless Elymas the sorcerer who opposed the truth (Acts 13:8-13), while he was content with dialogue with Peter and Barnabas.

21.10.2.en: Solomon the wise had already presented the same concept in his saying: “Smite a scorner, and the fool will become wise: and reprove one that hath understanding, and he will understand knowledge” (Prov 19:25). And the Apostle Paul says: “Them that sin rebuke before all, that others also may fear” (1 Tim 5:20).

21.10.3.en: * Here is a dilemma that often occurs. If you punish a man, perhaps you destroy him; and if you do not punish him, perhaps you destroy another man. I add that I err in this matter every day.

21.10.4.en: St. Augustine * False tenderness toward the wicked is a betrayal of the truth, an excuse for society, and a means for a man to become accustomed to tolerating evil... “Them that sin rebuke,” says the Apostle, and he immediately added the reason, saying: “that others also may fear.”

21.11.0.en: St. Basil the Great The righteous man considers the house of the wicked, and overthrows the wicked for their wickedness [12].

21.11.1.en: Some scholars, such as Joseph Parker, see that the righteous one here is meant to be God Almighty, the Righteous One: with His long-suffering toward the wicked and all the people of his house, He leaves him to prosper for a time, hoping he may repent, and if he does not repent, his evil returns upon him.

21.11.2.en: But some, such as Matthew Henry, see that the righteous one here is the righteous ruler or judge, for he examines the case of the wicked with all diligence and exactness so that when he judges him he does not wrong him.

21.11.3.en: In any case, the righteous man sees the house of the wicked prosper without being troubled or disturbed by his success, but insists on his fellowship with God whatever the cost, without turning aside with the wicked, and so he becomes a witness and judge against the wicked on the day of his collapse, on the great day of the Lord, or in the present life, because the success of the wicked will not last.

21.12.0.en: Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry himself, but shall not be heard [13].

21.12.1.en: In Proverbs 19:17 there is an assurance from God that he who has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord, who repays him this loan as a guarantor for His poor creature. Here He warns against stopping the ears at the cries of the poor, for his own cries will also not be answered.

21.12.2.en: * He who has no mercy cannot be made worthy of the mercies of God, and he who is not compassionate toward the petition of the poor does not obtain any petition of divine love by his prayers.

21.12.3.en: Martyr Cyprian * Alms given to the needy from the gains of injustice are not acceptable to God. Indeed he who refrains from practicing injustice but does not share with anyone the good things he owns is not worthy of praise... If you offer to God from the fruits of injustice and plunder, it would have been better for you not to possess such wealth than to possess it and give an offering.

21.12.4.en: St. Basil the Great * Do you not agree that poverty, as I have said, is more cruel than any beast of prey? Therefore you must help those who fall under it.

21.12.5.en: Incline your ears to the poor, and listen to them, as it is written: “Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry himself, but shall not be heard” (Prov 21:13). Give that you may receive, hear that you may be heard, sow the little that you have and you will reap much. Besides this, the pleasure of the body is meager and temporary and ends in corruption. But he who practices giving and love for the poor is crowned with glory from God, and they lead him to the incorruptible happiness that Christ gives to those who love Him.

21.12.6.en: St. Cyril the Great * The remedy for propitiating God has been given to us in the words of God Himself, for the divine teachings instruct sinners what they must do, which is that God is content with works of righteousness (through the blood of Christ). By mercy they deserve forgiveness of sin. It is written in Solomon: “Shut up alms in thy storehouses (in the heart of the poor): and it shall deliver thee from all affliction” (Sir 29:15).

21.12.7.en: And also: “Whoso stoppeth his ears at the cry of the poor, he also shall cry himself, but shall not be heard” (Prov 21:13). For he who has no mercy cannot be made worthy of the mercies of the Lord. And he who has no humanity toward the petitions of the poor draws by his prayers no share of divine compassion. This is what the Holy Spirit declared in the Psalms, affirming: “Blessed is he that considereth the poor: the LORD will deliver him in time of trouble” (Ps 41:1).

21.12.8.en: Remember what commandment Daniel gave to King Nebuchadnezzar when he was anxious and afraid of the terrible dream, offering him a remedy to obtain divine help that removes evils, as he says to him: “Wherefore, O king, let my counsel be acceptable unto thee, and break off thy sins by righteousness, and thine iniquities by shewing mercy to the poor...” And since the king did not obey him, he fell under the calamities and evils which he had seen, which he could have escaped by almsgiving.

21.12.9.en: The angel Raphael testifies to the same, urging the giving of alms by choice and generosity, as he says: “Prayer is good with fasting and alms: for alms doth deliver from death, and shall purge away all sin” (Tob 12:8-9). He shows that our prayers and fasts, unless alms assist them, become less profitable. For he who does them without supporting them with good works, their power is weak in attaining his petition.

21.12.10.en: The angel declared, made clear and testified that by almsgiving our supplications become effective, life becomes free of danger, and the spirit is delivered from death.

21.13.0.en: 14 A gift in secret pacifieth anger: and a reward in the bosom strong wrath. 15 It is joy to the just to do judgment: but destruction shall be to the workers of iniquity. 16 The man that wandereth out of the way of understanding shall remain in the company of the phantoms. 17 He that loveth pleasure shall be a poor man: he that loveth wine and oil shall not be rich. 18 The wicked shall be a ransom for the righteous, and the transgressor for the upright. 19 It is better to dwell in the wilderness, than with a contentious and an angry woman. 20 There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up. 21 He that followeth after righteousness and mercy findeth life, fortune and honour. 22 A wise man scaleth the city of the mighty, and casteth down the strength of the confidence thereof. 23 Whoso keepeth his mouth and his tongue keepeth his soul from troubles. 24 The swollen, proud one, his name is “scorner,” acting in an overflow of pride. 25 The desire of the slothful killeth him; for his hands refuse to labour. 26 He coveteth greedily all the day long: but the righteous giveth and spareth not. 27 The sacrifice of the wicked is abomination: how much more, when he bringeth it with deceit! 28 A false witness shall perish: but the man that heareth the truth speaketh. 29 A wicked man hardeneth his face: but as for the upright, he establisheth his ways. 30 There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the LORD.

21.13.1.en: A gift in secret pacifieth anger: and a reward in the bosom strong wrath [14].

21.13.2.en: Nothing calms a man’s anger like offering a gift to the one who is angry with him, provided it is offered with a pure mind and a sincere intention, accompanied by a spirit of humility and the Lord’s support for him. It is offered in secret, not openly, which would make the angry person doubt the intention of the giver. Perhaps by offering it in secret he does not give the wicked an opportunity to distort this work.

21.13.3.en: Offering gifts in a good spirit, even among the members of the family, gives better peace than much dialogue and argument and a man’s defending himself. But he who offers the gift as a bribe to corrupt justice and to obtain what he has no right to, it is shameful and disgraceful.

21.13.4.en: St. Evagrius links the material gift with sincere intention and an upright life.

21.13.5.en: * “The gift of man” is called the upright life. This gift makes a place for him, and qualifies him for all the fullness of God (Eph 3:19). It is the very thing that is called the throne of the holy powers. Truly the throne of the mind is the exalted state which is reached by those who sit in a steadfast, unshakable state.

21.14.0.en: St. Evagrius It is joy to the just to do judgment: but destruction shall be to the workers of iniquity [15].

21.14.1.en: The righteous rejoices in the truth even if there is a temporary loss in it, for he trusts in God’s reward to him. But the wicked is not in harmony with the truth, for his evil appears before him and he fears the punishment he expects.

21.14.2.en: The honest businessman, though he passes through financial difficulties, will succeed, but the deceiver and the wicked, though he gains much, will lose all that he gathered unjustly.

21.14.3.en: The righteous rejoice at the realization of justice in the courts and on the part of the ruler, but the wicked fears it lest the day of judgment come against him!

21.14.4.en: The righteous does not admire the success of the wicked and their conduct, whatever their social position, or his kinship to him or friendship with him. He admires justice and righteousness, therefore it was said: “It is not good to accept the person of the wicked” (Prov 18:5).

21.14.5.en: * It is not good to admire the wicked, even if one of them has an important position, or covers what is right with persuasive speech. He who admires the conduct of the wicked acknowledges the iniquity that Satan inspires.

21.15.0.en: St. John Chrysostom The man that wandereth out of the way of understanding shall remain in the company of the phantoms [16].

21.15.1.en: He who strays from the way of truth loses the taste of life, whatever honors or glories or possessions he obtains, and becomes like one who lives in the society of the evil spirits, the “phantoms,” or the society of the dead. This is what happened to Judas when he betrayed his Master, for he counted himself among the dead, and his suicide came as a real translation of what he was living within himself and imagining.

21.15.2.en: * It is a man’s error not to know the Scriptures; and he who knows them and neglects them errs doubly.

21.15.3.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian He that loveth pleasure shall be a poor man.

21.16.0.en: He that loveth wine and oil shall not be rich [17].

21.16.1.en: By “pleasure” here is meant immersion in worldly delights and joys, so that a man thinks that life has no taste without excess in pleasures, and so material poverty comes upon him, and the deprivation of inner joy. This was the fate of the prodigal son, but his returning to his father’s bosom saved him from what had befallen him.

21.16.2.en: He expressed this immersion in pleasures by the love of wine and exaggerated perfumes.

21.16.3.en: * The Holy Bible always uses wine in a mystical sense, as a symbol of the holy blood, and forbids any excess in its use.

21.16.4.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * All those who are being prepared to become disciples of Jesus must abstain from intoxicating wine.

21.16.5.en: St. Pachomius * Those who eat the heavenly bread become heavenly, without doubt! Wine teaches us that it makes those who are fond of it like itself, for it hates those who are devoted to it, and makes them drunk and in madness and an object of mockery.

21.16.6.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian * “He that loveth pleasure shall be a poor man: he that loveth wine and oil shall not be rich” (Prov 21:17).

21.16.7.en: It is perfectly clear that no one can approach the purity and cleanness of God without first being purified. Therefore we must set up high and strong partitions between ourselves and bodily pleasures, because when we approach God the purity of our hearts must not be defiled again. Those who have experience teach us that just as water is divided into many streams from a single brook, so pleasure spreads itself over those who love it through the senses and the ways leading to them. And the person who yields to pleasure through any sense has wounded himself by that sense. This agrees with the teaching of Christ: whoever consents to pleasure through the eye has received sin in the heart. Therefore we can add to His saying: he who hears... he who touches, or who uses any sense to serve his pleasures has sinned in his heart... And to prevent this we must control ourselves and our lives. We must not let our minds dwell where lust falls. In everything we do we must choose what benefits us, and leave the rest which may harm the senses.

21.17.0.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa The wicked shall be a ransom for the righteous, and the transgressor for the upright [18].

21.17.1.en: Justice requires the punishment of the wicked criminal, so that the righteous or just man is saved, and the treacherous must be punished so that the upright may find a place of rest.

21.17.2.en: Perhaps he refers here to removing the evil leaven so that it does not corrupt the whole lump. Joshua the son of Nun was compelled to punish Achan the son of Zerah so that the Lord might turn from the fierceness of His anger (Josh 7:17-26). And Phinehas the priest destroyed the Israelite man together with the pagan Midianite woman who had entered the tent of meeting, and the plague was stayed from the people (Num 25:6-11).

21.17.3.en: * Beloved, from your youth choose discipline, and you will find it in your old age to be mind and understanding.

21.17.4.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian Thanks be to God, who in His love gave His holy Son to grant us His righteousness, so that the incarnate Word of God became a sin offering for us.

21.18.0.en: It is better to dwell in the wilderness, than with a contentious and an angry woman [19].

21.18.1.en: There is nothing more bitter than for a man to live in a house where there is strife, for dwelling in the corner of the housetop [9] or in a barren wilderness [19] is better than being in a house where there is strife.

21.18.2.en: * “It is better to dwell in the wilderness, than with a contentious and an angry woman” (Prov 21:19). Therefore, O wives, show your godliness by your humility and meekness to all who are outside the Church, whether men or women, for their guidance and progress in the faith. And as we warn you and instruct you briefly, since we regard you as sisters and daughters and members of us, walk in wisdom, and keep yourselves in the way of life without blame. Seek to know such a kind of learning by which you may attain to the kingdom of our Lord and please Him, and rest forever and ever.

21.19.0.en: Canons of the Apostles There is treasure to be desired and oil in the dwelling of the wise; but a foolish man spendeth it up [20].

21.19.1.en: The wise man looks to the future, so that when his ability to work weakens he finds what he stored up in the days of his youth, he finds the lamp of his life not lacking oil. But the fool is wasteful in amusement, and squanders what he earned, and falls into want. Thus live the children of God, as they look to the eternal future and gather treasures through the work of divine grace in love for God and for neighbor, so that when the heavenly Bridegroom comes He finds a place for him with the wise virgins who take oil in their vessels with their lamps, and he enters the heavenly wedding (Mt 25:4-7).

21.19.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) sees that by the treasure here are understood the gifts presented by the Magi of gold, frankincense and myrrh, spiritual gifts. Gold points to offering the word of wisdom issuing from the believer’s understanding, frankincense is prayer, and myrrh is the mortification of the body.

21.19.3.en: * There is more to be understood concerning gold, incense, frankincense and myrrh. Solomon testifies that gold symbolizes wisdom when he says: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov 21:20) LXX. The psalmist testifies of incense that it is the prayer offered to God, as he says: “Let my prayer be set forth as incense before thee” (Ps 140:2) LXX. And myrrh points to the mortification of our bodies, where the holy Church speaks of those who labor in it, who strive unto death for God’s sake: “My hands dropped with myrrh.” Thus we offer gold when we shine before His eyes with the splendor of the wisdom from above. And we also offer Him incense if we burn on the altar of our hearts our human thoughts by persevering in prayer, so that a sweet fragrance is offered which God smells in our heavenly desires. And we offer myrrh if we put to death the vices of our bodies by self-denial.

21.19.5.en: * (Concerning clean and unclean animals) Thus those who hear carelessly may be said to swallow what they hear, so that they no longer taste it in their mouths, but bury what they hear under forgetfulness. But those who meditate on the law of the Lord day and night (Ps 1:2) ruminate on it, like those who enjoy the flavor of the word by a kind of sense of taste in the heart.

21.20.0.en: St. Augustine He that followeth after righteousness and mercy findeth life, fortune and honour [21].

21.20.1.en: By fellowship with the Holy One, the believer enjoys the righteousness of Christ and delights in the mark of mercy, and so rises as though from death to life, and from the shame of sin to the honor of the children of God and their glory. Righteousness and mercy raise the banner of the believer and even of nations, while sin brings man down to the pit and eternal shame.

21.21.0.en: A wise man scaleth the city of the mighty, and casteth down the strength of the confidence thereof [22].

21.21.1.en: Wisdom is above strength, for how many great nations relied on their fortresses and armies and abilities, yet collapsed before wise men.

21.21.2.en: If the enemy of good thinks of himself as the prince of this world, he collapsed by the wisdom of the Cross, for by it He “spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them” (Col 2:15).

21.21.3.en: * “A wise man attacks strong cities, and destroys the strongholds in which the wicked trust” (cf. Prov 21:22)? Do you think that when Solomon said this he wanted to teach us that the wise man attacks cities and destroys strongholds built of stones? Rather he refers to the city and the walls, which are the teachings of the wicked and the logical syllogisms of the philosophers, by which they add every evil contrary to the divine law, and which are practiced by the pagans and the barbarians, and those things which the heretics set up as proofs drawn from the Holy Bible like high mountains. These also must be counted among the fortified cities built on the mountains; such cities are destroyed by the wise man who proclaims the word of truth.

21.22.0.en: Origen Whoso keepeth his mouth and his tongue keepeth his soul from troubles [23].

21.22.1.en: The book of Proverbs, indeed the Holy Bible as a whole, often repeats the necessity of controlling the tongue and sanctifying the mouth, so that the psalmist cries out asking for divine guard over his mouth: “Set a watch, O LORD, before my mouth; keep the door of my lips.” With every morning the believer renews this petition in the prayer of Prime.

21.22.2.en: * The tongue stands in the middle, ready for either use, and you are its master. So also the sword lies in the middle: if you use it against the enemy it becomes an instrument of your deliverance, and if you wound yourself with it, it becomes the cause of your death, not the sword but your disobedience to the law. Let us think of the tongue in the same way, as a sword in the middle. Make it sharp to accuse yourself of your sins, and do not use it to wound your brother.
